title: Putting a Number on the Wobble

steps.body:
The width of the pile has a formula. For a proportion, the **standard error** is

SE = √( p(1−p) / n ).

It is the typical distance between a poll and the truth. And about 95% of the pile sits within **two** standard errors of the centre — the fact the rest of this course is built on.

explanationVariants: With p = 0.5 the numerator is 0.25, and 0.25/100 = 0.0025. Its square root is 0.05.

widget.prompt: A poll of 100 people, with p = 0.5. Find the standard error, in **percentage points**.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the SE as a decimal — correct arithmetic, wrong units. As a percentage of the population it is 5 points, not 0.05 points.
That is 0.25 as a percentage: you stopped at p(1−p) and skipped both the division by n and the square root.
That is half the SE — most likely a stray division. √(0.25/100) = 0.05 = 5 points.

steps.body: Two standard errors, in both directions.

panels.title: The pile is bell-shaped
panels.body: Add up enough independent coin-flips and the pile of results takes on the same bell shape every time. That is why one formula covers so many situations.

panels.title: Two SEs each way
panels.body: For a bell, about 95% of the area lies within two standard errors of the centre. So about 19 polls in 20 land within 2 × SE of the truth.

panels.title: Turn it around
panels.body: If 19 polls in 20 land within 2 SE of the truth, then for 19 polls in 20 the truth lies within 2 SE of the POLL. That flip is what lets one poll say something about a population.

widget.continueFeedback: Keep going — the last panel is the whole trick.
widget.successFeedback: That flip — from 'the poll is near the truth' to 'the truth is near the poll' — is what turns a single sample into an interval.

explanationVariants: 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.24, and 0.24/600 = 0.0004, whose square root is 0.02. Double it for the 95% band.

widget.prompt: A poll of 600 people gives p̂ = 0.60. Find **2 × SE**, in percentage points.

commonErrors.feedback: That is one SE (0.02 = 2 points). The 95% band is TWO standard errors wide on each side.
That is 4 × SE. About 95% of polls fall within two SEs, not four.
That is p(1−p) = 0.24 read as a percentage — the calculation stopped before dividing by n and taking the root.

steps.body:
Two practical facts fall out of the formula.

**p(1−p) is largest at p = 0.5.** A 50/50 split is the hardest to pin down, so pollsters quote the worst case to be safe.

**n is under the square root.** The wobble depends on the SIZE of the sample, not on the size of the population — polling 1,000 people works as well for a city as for a country.

explanationVariants: The population size does not appear anywhere in SE = √(p(1−p)/n). Only n does.
A spoonful is enough to taste a pot or a vat, provided it is stirred. The sample size is what matters, not what fraction of the population it is.

widget.prompt: A 1,000-person poll is run in a city of 100,000 and again in a country of 100 million. Which has the smaller wobble?

options.label: Neither — the wobble depends on n, not on the population size.
options.feedback: Right, and it surprises almost everyone. Only n appears in the formula. A well-stirred spoonful tastes the pot and the vat equally well.

options.label: The city poll, because 1,000 is a bigger share of 100,000.
options.feedback: Intuitive, and wrong. The share of the population you sampled does not enter the formula — √(p(1−p)/n) contains no N at all.

options.label: The country poll, because bigger populations average out.
options.feedback: Populations do not average anything out for you. The only averaging happens inside your sample, and both samples are 1,000.

options.label: The city poll, because there is less variety among people.
options.feedback: That is an assumption about the population, not something the design guarantees. And the formula does not contain population variety either — only p and n.

hints: Pollsters do not know p in advance, so they plan for the value of p that makes p(1−p) largest.
Try p = 0.5, p = 0.3 and p = 0.1: p(1−p) gives 0.25, 0.21 and 0.09. The maximum is at 0.5.
So use p = 0.5 and n = 1000: SE = √(0.25/1000), then double it and convert to percentage points.
explanationVariants: Worst case p = 0.5 gives SE = √(0.25/1000) ≈ 0.0158, so 2 SE ≈ 0.0316 ≈ 3.2 percentage points — the famous ±3 on a 1,000-person poll.
p(1−p) peaks at 0.25 when p = 0.5, so no true value could make this poll wobble more than about ±3.2 points.

widget.prompt: A pollster surveys 1,000 people and quotes the WORST-CASE 2-SE margin. What is it, in percentage points (one decimal)?

commonErrors.feedback: That is one SE (about 1.58 points). The quoted margin is two of them.
That is 4 × SE. The convention is a 2-SE band, which covers about 95% of the pile.
That is the margin as a decimal (0.0316). In percentage points it is 3.2.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Worst case p = 0.5: SE = √(0.25/1000) ≈ 0.0158, so 2 SE ≈ 3.2 percentage points.

takeaways: SE = √(p(1−p)/n) is the typical distance from a poll to the truth; about 95% of polls land within 2 SE of it.
p(1−p) peaks at p = 0.5, so pollsters quote that worst case — which is where the familiar ±3 on a 1,000-person poll comes from.
The wobble depends on the sample size, never on the population size.
steps.teaser: Next chapter: turn that band around and point it at the truth.

concept.body: Work the formula in order. First p(1−p). Then divide by n. Then take the square root — that is one SE. Then double it for the 95% band. Skipping the square root is the most common slip, and it inflates the answer enormously.

explanationVariants: SE = 0.025, so the poll typically lands within about 2.5 points of the truth — and within 5 points about 95% of the time.

widget.prompt: p = 0.5, n = 400. Find the standard error in percentage points.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 2 × SE, the 95% band. One standard error is half of it: 2.5 points.
That is p(1−p) = 0.25 read as a percent — the division by n and the square root are both still to come.
